newsitem.title: USA: Transportation chief outlines Clinton ISTEA plan.
newsitem.headline: Transportation chief outlines Clinton ISTEA plan.

text.p: U.S. Transportation Secretary Rodney Slater on Wednesday said that the Clinton Administration supports a new six-year, $174 billion investment program for American highways, public transit and other surface transportation.

Slater's testimony before a key Senate subcommittee was his first regarding reauthorization of the Intermodal Surface Transportation Efficiency Act of 1991 (ISTEA) since being sworn in as DOT's chief on Feb 14. ISTEA expires Sept 30.

The President's plan, called the National Economic Crossroads Transportation Efficiency Act (NEXTEA), would reauthorize expiring ISTEA programs through 2003. The President is expected to send the plan to Congress shortly.

The proposal, an 11 percent increase over current ISTEA funding levels, would continue to fund the state infrastructure bank program at $150 million and expand it by opening it to all states, Slater said.

Sen. John Chaffee, R-R.I., chairman of the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee, lauded the Clinton plan, saying it give states and localities flexibility while setting strong national standards.
But he expressed concern that the Clinton bill apparently would use "gas tax contributions" as the primary way of distributing funds to states.
"Under a tax-driven scenario, states that use the most gas receive more money and are wrongly perceived to have greater needs than states that move people and goods more efficiently," Chaffee warned.
Sen. John Warner, R-Va., chairman of the Environment and Public Works Committee's subpanel on transportation and infrastructure, which conducted Wednesday's hearing, slammed the upcoming bill.
"It falls short of reflecting the proper role of leadership for the President. We need active leadership," Warner said.
Warner backs a a bill sponosred by House Majority Whip Tom Delay, R-Texas, dubbed STEP 21.

It would guarantee that all states get at least 95 percent of what they contribute to the federal program. States currently are promised an 89 percent return, but some states get less because of exceptions built into the rule.

Slater outlined other key provisions of the President's upcoming proposal. He said the bill would set up a $100 million federal credit program to fund multi-state transportation projects of "national significance" - projects that a single state might not be able to manage alone.
Slater said the upcoming plan would keep successful "core" programs of ISTEA, like the 165,000 mile National Highway System, the maintenance of interstate highways, and bridge construction.
It would improve air, rail and port access to the "global marketplace" by improving connections to the national highway system, he said.
It also would improving border crossing and major "trade corridors" in the wake of the North American Free Trade Agreement (NAFTA) and the General Agreement of Tarriffs and Trade (GATT), Slater said.
Slater said the plan would dedicate $500 million to improve highway safety and to reward states that have a certain mix of infrastructure safety programs.

He said the plan would make it easier for state and local transportation officials to target dollars to high priority projects. It also would authorize funds for a highway development prgram for Appalachian states, he said.
The bill also would give rural towns and small cities with under 200,000 people more flexibility to spend federal transit money, Slater said.
